title: Assess lithium during volume loss
stem: A client taking lithium has gastroenteritis, coarse tremor and unsteady walking. The usual evening dose is due. What is most appropriate?
options: Use last month's normal lithium result to guide tonight's dose
Withhold pending prompt toxicity and hydration assessment
Give the dose after an oral rehydration drink
Treat the tremor with the usual anxiety PRN medicine
why: An old result does not reflect the current illness and clearance changes.
Fluid loss can reduce lithium clearance, and the new neurological signs suggest toxicity.
One drink does not resolve possible accumulated lithium or neurological toxicity.
Symptom suppression can obscure assessment without addressing lithium exposure.
takeaway: Fluid loss can reduce lithium clearance, and the new neurological signs suggest toxicity.
learningObjective: Integrate gastrointestinal losses, neurological changes and renal clearance when assessing possible lithium toxicity.

title: Plan stable intake with lithium
stem: A client stable on lithium plans a low-sodium weight-loss diet and strenuous outdoor exercise. What is the most relevant teaching?
options: Increase dietary restriction gradually without mentioning lithium
Use extra coffee to replace fluids lost during exercise
Review sodium and fluid changes with the treatment team
Keep the same lithium dose but monitor only body weight
why: Gradual change can still affect lithium handling and needs coordination.
This is not an individualized hydration plan and may complicate fluid balance.
Sweating and major sodium changes can alter lithium concentrations.
Weight alone does not assess lithium exposure or hydration safety.
takeaway: Sweating and major sodium changes can alter lithium concentrations.
learningObjective: Explain why major sodium and fluid changes warrant review during lithium therapy.

title: Review a new lithium interaction
stem: A client on lithium receives a new hydrochlorothiazide prescription. The pharmacist flags possible increased lithium exposure. What should the nurse ensure?
options: Separate the medicines between morning and evening only
Rely on monitoring only if the client first develops tremor
Review only thyroid results because lithium can affect thyroid function
An interaction review and level-monitoring plan
why: Spacing does not remove the renal interaction.
Waiting for toxicity symptoms is less safe than planned monitoring.
Thyroid monitoring does not address the new renal interaction affecting lithium concentrations.
Thiazides can increase lithium concentrations, requiring an authorized management plan.
takeaway: Thiazides can increase lithium concentrations, requiring an authorized management plan.
learningObjective: Identify a need for lithium monitoring when a thiazide is added.

title: Assess early antidepressant activation
stem: One week after starting an antidepressant, a client reports marked restlessness and new thoughts of self-harm. What is the priority?
options: Assess immediate safety and arrange urgent clinical review
Explain that full mood benefit takes weeks and review then
Recommend changing the administration time as the only intervention
Focus first on measuring appetite and sleep improvement
why: New self-harm thoughts and activation require timely risk assessment and support.
Delayed therapeutic benefit does not justify postponing current safety assessment.
Timing adjustment alone does not address the new self-harm risk.
Those outcomes matter, but the stated safety concern takes priority.
takeaway: New self-harm thoughts and activation require timely risk assessment and support.
learningObjective: Assess new agitation and self-harm risk soon after antidepressant initiation.

title: Identify serotonin toxicity
stem: A client taking an SSRI starts tramadol and develops agitation, sweating, diarrhea and marked tremor. What is most appropriate?
options: Attribute the symptoms to antidepressant withdrawal without checking use
Urgent assessment of possible serotonin toxicity
Treat diarrhea first and leave medication review until tomorrow
Give the next tramadol dose to relieve associated aches
why: The reported new exposure better supports an interaction needing assessment.
The new combination and symptom cluster warrant prompt evaluation.
A systemic interaction may progress while one symptom is treated.
Further serotonergic exposure may worsen the suspected syndrome.
takeaway: The new combination and symptom cluster warrant prompt evaluation.
learningObjective: Recognize a concerning autonomic and neuromuscular pattern after serotonergic medicines are combined.

title: Recognize antipsychotic-related hyperthermia
stem: After an antipsychotic increase, a client develops high fever, generalized rigidity, confusion and unstable blood pressure. What concern requires immediate escalation?
options: Infection alone, without considering the recent drug increase
A mild movement effect that can wait for the next dose review
Possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Isolated akathisia needing only routine symptom review
why: Infection remains a differential, but the rigidity and medication change require urgent consideration of drug toxicity.
The systemic deterioration requires immediate assessment rather than routine follow-up.
The medication change and systemic rigidity pattern indicate a potential medical emergency.
Akathisia does not explain marked fever, rigidity and autonomic instability.
takeaway: The medication change and systemic rigidity pattern indicate a potential medical emergency.
learningObjective: Differentiate a severe rigidity and hyperthermia syndrome from routine agitation after antipsychotic treatment.

title: Recognize acute dystonia
stem: A client recently given a dopamine-blocking antiemetic develops painful neck twisting and difficulty opening the jaw. What is appropriate?
options: Encourage neck stretching before reviewing the medication
Interpret it as chronic tardive dyskinesia without considering timing
Give another antiemetic dose because nausea is still present
Assess airway safety and obtain prompt treatment for possible dystonia
why: Forced movement may worsen distress and delays targeted assessment.
The abrupt onset after recent exposure supports an acute reaction.
Further dopamine blockade may worsen the suspected reaction.
An acute muscle contraction can involve structures affecting breathing or swallowing.
takeaway: An acute muscle contraction can involve structures affecting breathing or swallowing.
learningObjective: Respond to acute involuntary neck and jaw contraction after dopamine-blocking medication.

title: Distinguish akathisia from worsening psychosis
stem: After an antipsychotic increase, a client paces and says, 'I cannot keep still inside.' Hallucinations have decreased. What is most appropriate?
options: Assess and report possible akathisia
Request another increase because pacing proves psychosis is worse
Ask the client to remain seated before discussing symptoms
Record the pacing only as refusal to participate
why: New inner restlessness after dose escalation suggests a movement adverse effect.
The improved hallucinations and timing argue against that assumption.
This does not address the distressing involuntary restlessness.
That interpretation overlooks a potentially treatable medication effect.
takeaway: New inner restlessness after dose escalation suggests a movement adverse effect.
learningObjective: Recognize medication-related inner restlessness before assuming a need for more antipsychotic.

title: Evaluate new repetitive movements
stem: A client on long-term antipsychotic therapy develops repetitive lip smacking and tongue movements. What should the nurse do?
options: Wait until the movements interfere with eating to report
Document the movements and arrange timely medication review
Treat it as an acute panic episode because movements are repetitive
Recommend simply increasing the current antipsychotic
why: Earlier recognition supports review before greater functional impairment.
The pattern may represent tardive dyskinesia requiring treatment reassessment.
The movement pattern and prolonged exposure warrant a drug-effect assessment.
A dose increase can obscure movements without addressing the underlying complication.
takeaway: The pattern may represent tardive dyskinesia requiring treatment reassessment.
learningObjective: Recognize possible tardive dyskinesia during prolonged antipsychotic exposure.

title: Respond to infection symptoms during clozapine therapy
stem: A client taking clozapine develops fever and a sore throat. Their last blood count was acceptable two weeks ago. What is appropriate?
options: Treat with an available cold remedy and report only persistent symptoms
Focus only on whether hallucinations remain controlled
Prompt clinical review and current blood-count assessment
Use the earlier result to defer review until the next scheduled test
why: Symptomatic treatment alone can delay detection of a serious complication.
Psychiatric improvement does not establish hematological safety.
A previous acceptable count does not exclude newly developed neutropenia.
Blood counts can change between scheduled tests.
takeaway: A previous acceptable count does not exclude newly developed neutropenia.
learningObjective: Promptly assess possible neutropenia when infection symptoms develop during clozapine use.

title: Recognize severe clozapine-related constipation
stem: A client taking clozapine has no bowel movement for several days, increasing abdominal distension and vomiting. What should happen?
options: Offer the usual fibre supplement and review next week
Assume reduced intake fully explains the bowel change
Wait until severe pain appears before calling the team
Urgent abdominal assessment before routine oral laxative measures
why: Distension and vomiting warrant more urgent assessment than routine constipation advice.
The medication and severe associated symptoms raise additional concern.
Serious hypomotility may progress without proportionate reported pain.
Clozapine hypomotility can progress to serious obstruction or ileus.
takeaway: Clozapine hypomotility can progress to serious obstruction or ileus.
learningObjective: Escalate possible gastrointestinal hypomotility when constipation is accompanied by systemic abdominal symptoms.

title: Coordinate levodopa with meal effects
stem: A client taking levodopa reports worse mobility after large protein-rich meals but needs adequate nutrition. What is most useful?
options: Review medication timing and protein distribution with the team
Remove protein from the diet without dietary review
Take extra levodopa after every large meal
Assume worsening mobility means the diagnosis was incorrect
why: A coordinated plan can address absorption effects while preserving nutrition.
Broad elimination risks poor nutrition and is not an individualized plan.
Unprescribed dose increases can produce adverse effects.
Meal-related response changes can occur within established Parkinson disease.
takeaway: A coordinated plan can address absorption effects while preserving nutrition.
learningObjective: Address a reproducible meal-related levodopa response without unnecessary protein restriction.

title: Assess wearing-off symptoms
stem: A client moves well after levodopa but develops predictable stiffness shortly before each next dose. What information is most useful to record?
options: A single symptom rating unrelated to administration time
Dose times and the onset and duration of symptom changes
Only the total number of tablets taken each week
Only the client's best walking performance after a dose
why: Without timing, the pattern guiding treatment remains unclear.
A timing diary helps identify wearing-off and guide regimen review.
A weekly total misses the relationship between doses and symptoms.
Peak function does not capture end-of-dose deterioration.
takeaway: A timing diary helps identify wearing-off and guide regimen review.
learningObjective: Use the timing of symptom recurrence to support Parkinson medication review.

title: Teach phenytoin oral care
stem: A client starting long-term phenytoin asks about gum changes mentioned in teaching. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Use mouthwash alone instead of mechanical cleaning
Stop phenytoin independently if gums bleed during brushing
Regular gentle oral care and dental follow-up
Avoid brushing areas that begin to enlarge
why: Rinsing alone does not adequately remove plaque.
Seizure treatment changes require review rather than abrupt withdrawal.
Good hygiene and dental assessment help manage gingival overgrowth risk.
Avoidance can worsen plaque accumulation and inflammation.
takeaway: Good hygiene and dental assessment help manage gingival overgrowth risk.
learningObjective: Support prevention and early recognition of gingival complications during phenytoin therapy.

title: Assess possible benzodiazepine withdrawal
stem: A client who took a benzodiazepine regularly for months has missed it for several days and now has tremor, insomnia and marked anxiety. What is appropriate?
options: Treat the symptoms as confirmed recurrence of the original anxiety only
Arrange routine anxiety follow-up without communicating the missed doses
Defer review until the client has slept normally for a night
Assess withdrawal risk and obtain an urgent medication plan
why: Withdrawal must be considered given the clear interruption history.
Omitting the interruption history can obscure the need for timely withdrawal assessment.
Waiting may allow worsening withdrawal without treatment.
Abrupt interruption after regular use can cause significant withdrawal, including seizures.
takeaway: Abrupt interruption after regular use can cause significant withdrawal, including seizures.
learningObjective: Connect abrupt interruption of regular benzodiazepine use with withdrawal symptoms and seizure risk.

title: Monitor after naloxone response
stem: After naloxone, a client is awake and breathing adequately. The opioid involved may last longer than naloxone. What is appropriate?
options: Continue protocol-based respiratory monitoring for recurrence
Discontinue observation because the client can now speak
Give a sedative to prevent distress during observation
Use pain intensity as the only follow-up measure
why: Opioid effects can return as the reversal effect diminishes.
Speech at one time does not establish sustained recovery.
Further central depression can compromise respiratory safety.
Pain does not reliably assess recurrent ventilatory depression.
takeaway: Opioid effects can return as the reversal effect diminishes.
learningObjective: Explain why improved ventilation after naloxone does not end monitoring requirements.

title: Prevent heat-related fentanyl exposure
stem: A client wearing a fentanyl patch plans to use a heating pad over the painful shoulder where the patch is placed. What should the nurse advise?
options: Cut the patch before using the heating pad
Avoid direct heat over the patch and discuss another comfort measure
Use heat only after covering the patch with another dressing
Reduce the heat setting and monitor only local skin redness
why: Altering the patch does not safely compensate for heat exposure.
Heat can increase fentanyl absorption and overdose risk.
A covering does not establish protection against increased absorption.
Absorption can increase without a visible skin injury.
takeaway: Heat can increase fentanyl absorption and overdose risk.
learningObjective: Recognize external heat as a factor that can increase transdermal fentanyl absorption.

title: Explain patient-only PCA activation
stem: A visitor presses a sleeping client's PCA button to prevent pain on waking. What is the best response?
options: Permit presses only near the end of the lockout interval
Ask the visitor to use the client's pain history to decide
Explain that only the client should activate this PCA button
Permit it if the visitor records each button press
why: Lockout timing does not make proxy dosing safe.
Predicted pain cannot replace current patient-controlled use and assessment.
The client's inability to self-activate while deeply sedated is a safety feature.
Documentation does not preserve the patient-controlled safety mechanism.
takeaway: The client's inability to self-activate while deeply sedated is a safety feature.
learningObjective: Preserve the patient-controlled analgesia safety mechanism by preventing family activation.

title: Plan for opioid-induced constipation
stem: A client starting regular opioid therapy has a history of constipation. What should the nurse prioritize in the ongoing plan?
options: Wait until severe abdominal pain develops before discussing a regimen
Rely on increased fibre alone despite limited fluid intake
Assume bowel effects will disappear when analgesic tolerance develops
Review a preventive bowel regimen and monitor bowel function
why: Delayed treatment can permit significant constipation or impaction.
Fibre without adequate fluid or a tailored plan may be insufficient.
Tolerance to analgesia does not reliably eliminate opioid constipation.
Constipation often persists during opioid use and benefits from anticipatory management.
takeaway: Constipation often persists during opioid use and benefits from anticipatory management.
learningObjective: Anticipate bowel effects when regular opioid treatment begins.

title: Detect duplicate acetaminophen products
stem: A client takes prescribed acetaminophen and a cold remedy whose label also lists acetaminophen. What should the nurse do?
options: Review the combined dose and advise a safe product plan
Check only the prescribed product's daily amount
Separate the products by one hour without reviewing totals
Recommend the cold remedy because combination products contain less risk
why: Different product names can conceal duplication of the same active ingredient.
The nonprescription ingredient also contributes to cumulative exposure.
Spacing does not eliminate total daily exposure.
Combination packaging does not protect against ingredient duplication.
takeaway: Different product names can conceal duplication of the same active ingredient.
learningObjective: Identify overlapping active ingredients across prescription and nonprescription analgesic products.

title: Assess NSAID use during dehydration
stem: A client taking naproxen develops vomiting, low intake and markedly reduced urine output. What is appropriate?
options: Wait for blood in the urine before reporting
Promptly assess hydration and kidney function and review naproxen
Give naproxen with food as the only safety adjustment
Ask only about dysuria to decide whether the urine change needs review
why: Renal injury can occur without visible hematuria.
NSAID-related renal effects can be more concerning during volume depletion.
Food may reduce irritation but does not resolve the renal perfusion concern.
Renal hypoperfusion can reduce output without urinary infection symptoms.
takeaway: NSAID-related renal effects can be more concerning during volume depletion.
learningObjective: Review renal risk before continuing an NSAID during acute volume depletion.

title: Clarify methotrexate frequency
stem: A client takes oral methotrexate once weekly for rheumatoid arthritis. New transfer orders list the same dose daily. What should happen before administration?
options: Assume the daily order replaces the home schedule
Divide the weekly dose into daily portions independently
Clarify the frequency discrepancy with the prescribing team
Give today's dose and clarify before tomorrow
why: A transfer discrepancy involving high-risk frequency needs verification.
An improvised schedule is not an authorized regimen.
Inadvertent daily low-dose methotrexate can cause severe toxicity.
The intended weekly day and last administration must be established first.
takeaway: Inadvertent daily low-dose methotrexate can cause severe toxicity.
learningObjective: Detect a dangerous daily-versus-weekly discrepancy in low-dose methotrexate treatment.

title: Distinguish urate control from acute analgesia
stem: A client newly prescribed allopurinol expects immediate relief of a painful gout flare. What is the best explanation?
options: Pain relief should occur after the first tablet if the diagnosis is correct
Use extra allopurinol whenever the joint becomes painful
Wait for allopurinol to work before discussing current severe pain
It lowers urate over time; acute pain needs the prescribed flare plan
why: Lack of immediate relief does not invalidate the gout diagnosis.
Symptom-triggered dose escalation is not its prescribed role.
The acute flare can require separate timely treatment.
Long-term urate control does not provide immediate anti-inflammatory analgesia.
takeaway: Long-term urate control does not provide immediate anti-inflammatory analgesia.
learningObjective: Explain the different purposes of long-term urate lowering and prescribed acute-flare treatment.

title: Review an opioid conversion
stem: A client's opioid order changes from morphine to hydromorphone, with the same route and dosing interval. A colleague suggests retaining the same milligram dose. What should the nurse do?
options: Verify the prescribed conversion and client-specific dose with the team
Use the old milligram dose because the route is unchanged
Assess the old opioid response without comparing relative potency
Use a conversion chart as the final dose without individualized review
why: Different opioid potency and individual risk make milligram-for-milligram substitution unsafe.
An unchanged route does not make potency equivalent.
Previous pain control matters but does not establish the new medicine's equivalent dose.
Conversion estimates require review of cross-tolerance and client-specific risk.
takeaway: Different opioid potency and individual risk make milligram-for-milligram substitution unsafe.
learningObjective: Recognize that different opioids are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.

title: Evaluate analgesia with function and safety
stem: After an analgesic adjustment, which findings support an effective and tolerable plan? Select all that apply.
options: The client can cough and mobilize more comfortably
The client stays readily alert with stable breathing
The pain score is lower but the client is difficult to arouse
The client sleeps through all activities because of new drowsiness
The client avoids every movement despite an unchanged resting score
why: Improved useful function supports meaningful pain relief.
Analgesia should not require clinically important respiratory or sedation harm.
Reduced reported pain does not compensate for dangerous sedation.
Sedation-related inactivity is not the intended functional outcome.
A resting score alone misses inadequately controlled movement-related pain.
takeaway: Improved useful function supports meaningful pain relief.
learningObjective: Balance pain relief, function and adverse effects when evaluating an analgesic regimen.
